title: What You Need to Know About Cognitive Science
author: Dominic Salles
summary: Dominic Salles explains what retrieval practice, spaced retrieval, interleaving and elaboration are and then lays out how school leaders can make them happen across a curriculum rather than leaving it to individual teachers. He supplies training activities for each principle, such as rapid-fire questioning with lollipop sticks and a doubling-interval schedule of up to ten retrievals over a two-year course. The leadership half insists that heads of department plan the sequence, that it stay a standing agenda item, and that work be shared publicly in middle-leader meetings. This is a close call between Learning & Curriculum and Practice & Culture; it sits in Learning & Curriculum because the content driving the piece is the cognitive science and how it is built into curriculum design.
points: Retrieval practice means anything that forces students to pull answers from their own memory after teaching, not a do-now where they wait to be told.
Spacing works because the brain strengthens a memory when it is retrieved just as it is being forgotten, so intervals roughly double over a course.
Leaders cannot leave retrieval and spacing to individual teachers; the sequence must be planned across two years by heads of department.
Interleaving means finding similarities and differences between topics, which differs from simply spacing a different topic.
Making the work public in middle-leader meetings keeps it moving and spreads good solutions between departments.
quotes: The brain is 2% of your body mass, but burns at least 20% of the calories your body needs. Brains are expensive. Thinking is hard.
Ebbinghaus discovered that our brains make very weak neural pathways. If you learn something today, you will have forgotten about 95% of it in 60 days’ time.
Many teachers confuse interleaving with spacing. We assume it is the study of a different topic. So, we interrupt the teaching of Macbeth to have a few lessons on A Christmas Carol.
Questions like these are not just novel, but quite profound. They force students not just to retrieve knowledge, but to reorganise it or link it in meaningful ways.
Here a student learns something and applies it to their own lives, or something they already know. This is really a form of interleaving, but led by the learner.
